bet.text: Placement speed: an alpha robot with a tilted elevator showed that placing quickly was one of the most important things, so later versions were built to speed it up.

demand.text: On day 1 the team gave each action a points-per-second score and saw little reason to focus on one piece. It later realized that many Worlds matches would tie at 193, so auto points would quite likely decide them. Supercharging then meant this did not matter too much.

auto.text: The intake is on the back so the robot need not turn, and the AprilTag pose worked well for placing cubes.
The cone and cube floor intake allows two cones and a cube for a high link, instead of a preloaded cone and two cubes.

cycle.text: The robot takes pieces at a substation or over the wide back intake. The operator picks only the piece and level; the robot finds the closest open node, drives there and scores.
An observer's table gives it 2.6 auto and 9.7 teleop pieces a match in championship qualifying.

endgame.text: Forks drop onto the charge station. Pulling down from a slightly offset point lifts the front of the robot first, then pivots it.

fallback.text: In a hit with large impact torque the belted arm drive can skip teeth without putting the arm out of use, and then return to work.

changed.text: An alpha robot was built early to de-risk subsystems: an elevator the team had built in the off-season, strapped on at an angle. The gear ratio started slower and rose through the season.
Beta slides moved from an arm under the carriage to a flip-over arm.
Beta had a cube-only floor intake; the cone roller came later.
Changes found on beta went into gamma's CAD in week 4.

outcome.text: 40-9-0 in official play; finalist in the Curie division; ranked 4 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 79.28, Curie).

facts.text: The team site lists four MK4i modules with blue nitrile tread
A team member says in the release thread that it used WCP SwerveX instead

solves.text: Take cubes at the back of the robot, so it need not turn in auto

facts.text: Mecanum wheels move the cube against a plate to center it
The team site lists extending rollers based on the previous year's intake

functions.name: Cone intake

solves.text: A tipped cone taken in at the back would be placed upside down as the arm rotates; this turns it without another powered joint

functions.type: floating tubing-sprung roller added to the cube intake

facts.text: The pivot floats, held out by surgical tubing; the force of the roller motor rotates it down and pushes the cone to an angle the gripper can take
It collects cones across the full width, so the driver need not be nearly as precise
The rollers lock once a cone is far enough in, so the 2 in cone roller pivots around the 3 in polycarbonate roller to a hard stop
It needs no added motor, which would have put the robot over the weight limit
The cone roller spins opposite to every other intake roller, so its position was laid out to clear a cube being taken in
A commenter says the robot was fairly competent with sideways cones on the floor, provided the robot faced away from them

solves.text: Grip either piece, optimized for the single and double substations because the wide intake handles the floor

facts.text: Double wheels grab cones or cubes, and a beam break senses possession

functions.name: Arm

solves.text: Pivot back to take a cube from the rear intake and then pivot to score, with no pass-through

functions.type: single-pivot belted arm on the elevator

facts.text: Belts run from a belt box to the pivot, and cables route through the pivot so there is no cable chain
The team site lists a wrist that angles the end effector with two belts and pulleys
Beta slides: flip-over range of motion about
Beta slides: all-belted joint, 15 mm belts except a 9 mm first stage, smallest pulley 18 teeth in metal
Every stage is belted, with an absolute encoder at the final point of rotation

The final stage uses two large pulleys, because one could not sustain the maximum torque the motor's current limit allows; the team usually takes ratings from published belt charts, which it has found conservative

The team started from a mechanism calculator and a move time, recalled as something like a 90 degree profiled move in 500 ms; for calculators that ignore deceleration it usually modeled the first half, 45 degrees in 250 ms
Sizing to the current limit is a first-order approximation, the team says: the inertia and friction of gearbox and motor matter too, so a mechanism that gets beaten up needs margin
The two large pulleys are 3D printed in a carbon fiber reinforced filament; almost all the team's pulleys are printed except very small ones, which tend to be on the motors

cost.text: Beta slides: the belt box pulley locations force a 27 x 28 in drive base
Skipping teeth is not great for the belts over time

functions.name: Angled elevator

solves.text: Place cones and cubes with fewer degrees of freedom by extending at an angle

functions.type: tilted two-stage elevator with an overextending carriage

facts.text: Two stages, with a carriage that extends past the top of the second
Dyneema runs inside the tubes so it cannot catch; the team says it never snapped
The team site counts three carriages
Beta slides: elevator width about
7/64 in Dyneema is tied to a spool near the bottom, runs continuously through the tubes and is tied to the carriage; two Falcon 500s on a 5:1 reduction turn the spool
The bearing blocks are custom, based on WCP ones but easy to cut on a typical Omio CNC with a 4 mm end mill; making them in-house saved a lot of money

solves.text: Get the robot off the ground and hold it until the match ends

facts.text: Rotating the gearbox releases the forks through cams, and springs drop them onto the charge station
One motor does both with the cams and a string
A forum post says side forks free room on the charge station for other robots

functions.name: Auto placement

solves.text: Remove manual alignment from scoring so cycles are fast and consistent

functions.type: AprilTag pose plus Limelight on retroreflective tape

facts.text: Wheel odometry is combined with three AprilTag cameras, two at the sides and one in front, on an Orange Pi 5
A front Limelight on the reflective tape fine-tunes cone placement
A cone node counts as filled when its tape is blocked, and the robot picks the closest open node

functions.name: Underside electronics

solves.text: Reach the wiring without digging through the robot, and free the space above

functions.type: electronics mounted below the belly pan

facts.text: As long as the panel below is easy to remove, tipping the robot makes little difference; the team preferred this to its 2022 electronics above the belly pan

cost.text: The robot must be flipped each time

decisions.choice: Intake on the back of the robot
decisions.because: not having to turn in auto would be an advantage
decisions.instead_of: intaking and scoring on the same side, as many teams did

decisions.choice: Turn cones with a floating sprung roller
decisions.because: the arm would otherwise place them upside down

decisions.choice: Limelight on the tape for cones
decisions.because: something more accurate than the AprilTag pose was needed for cones
decisions.instead_of: AprilTags and odometry alone, which worked for cubes

decisions.choice: Forks that lift and then pivot
decisions.because: the team thought either motion alone would not get the robot off the ground and hold it until the match ended
teeth cannot skip, it was easier to package (it routes through the tubes, and the belt gearbox took up more space than the team liked), and its lower rigging mass helps the elevator accelerate
decisions.instead_of: a belted elevator, as on the 2022 project elevator used for the alpha robot
decisions.cost: the belted rigging was much simpler

decisions.because: gears that strip in an impact put a subsystem out for the match, while belts can skip and recover
decisions.cost: wear on the belts over time

decisions.because: two cones and a cube could then be placed in auto, which would quite likely decide the many Worlds matches tied at 193; supercharging meant this did not matter too much, but taking a tipped cone now and then still helped
decisions.instead_of: the kickoff choice not to collect cones from the floor

decisions.because: it was simpler, and the team already had an elevator on hand
decisions.instead_of: a telescoping (pink) arm or a double-jointed arm

decisions.choice: One master layout sketch that every subsystem's sketch derives from
decisions.because: it assigns space beforehand and prevents overlap; in 2022 the team spent considerable time getting subsystems to coexist

decisions.choice: Review recorded match logs (AdvantageKit logs viewed in AdvantageScope, not replayed through modified code)
decisions.because: they led the team to the fault: in division playoffs, no gyro data although the gyro still appeared in Phoenix Tuner, fixed before the next match; at the first event, a wrong auto heading target, traced to how the code flipped it
